evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

contextual_issues: Informal/unpaid care from family or friends is described (reported by 5.6% of EM patients and 53.3% of disseminated/late LB patients, with hours quantified) but, per Belgian economic-evaluation guidelines, was not assigned a monetary value.

Patient out-of-pocket amounts (e.g., €43.9 EM / €286 disseminated/late direct medical costs paid by patients, and €5 EM / €190 disseminated/late travel costs) are already components of the reported total direct medical and direct non-medical cost figures; they must not be added again on top of the €5.59 million national total.

The €5.59 million annual total combines ambulatory costs extrapolated from 2015-2017 average incidence with hospitalization costs extrapolated from a 2016-2018 average number of admissions - two different averaging windows folded into one 'annual' figure; the authors further note 2019 itself was an atypically low tick-bite year, so the true 2019 cost was probably lower than this estimate.

GP consultations for tick bites without confirmed LB (19,422/year, €510,806) and ambulatory LB serological-testing costs (€1,092,801, 2015-2017) refer to broader populations (people with tick bites or who received a test, not necessarily clinically diagnosed LB patients) and must not be pooled into the €5.59 million total LB cost-of-illness figure.

spec.title: Belgian Lyme Borreliosis Cost-of-Illness Explorer (Geebelen et al. 2022)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces the per-patient and national annual cost figures reported by a Belgian prospective cohort and hospital-registry cost-of-illness study of erythema migrans (EM, early Lyme rash) versus disseminated/late Lyme borreliosis (including post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, PTLDS). All figures are in 2019 euros, societal perspective, Belgium only, and capture costs only up to 6 months post-diagnosis (12 months for PTLDS patients). It omits informal/unpaid caregiving value, pediatric-specific costs, non-reimbursed hospital supplements (single room, food, ambulance), tick-bite prophylaxis costs, and any costs beyond the study's follow-up window. It does not model other countries, other currencies, or longer time horizons.

takeaway.patient: Using this Belgian study's own reported figures, a patient diagnosed with disseminated or late-stage Lyme disease had a typical total cost (medical care, travel, and lost income combined) several times higher than a patient diagnosed with the early rash stage (erythema migrans), and about a quarter of direct medical costs were not reimbursed by insurance in this cohort.
takeaway.care: This scenario shows that per-patient costs for disseminated/late-stage Lyme borreliosis far exceed those for early-stage erythema migrans in this Belgian cohort, and that Belgium's hospital coding system cannot separately capture EM or PTLDS hospital presentations - both findings are relevant to how early-detection pathways and diagnosis coding are structured.
takeaway.policy: This scenario reproduces the study's national annual cost estimate for Lyme borreliosis in Belgium by combining each disease-stage subgroup's own case count and per-patient cost, showing that disseminated/late-stage disease drives the majority of national cost despite being far less common than early-stage disease, and quantifies the reimbursed-versus-patient-paid cost split relevant to coverage policy.

patient: Review your own medical bills and insurance statements to see how much of your Lyme-related medical costs were reimbursed versus paid out of pocket, since this study found roughly a quarter of direct medical costs were not reimbursed in this Belgian cohort.

If you have questions about why your stage of diagnosis (early rash versus later/disseminated disease) affects your costs or care plan, consider raising this directly with your clinician in plain terms rather than assuming a specific cause.

If you or a family member provided unpaid caregiving time during treatment, know that this study documented such caregiving but did not assign it a dollar value, so your own experience of that burden may not be reflected in these cost figures.
care: This finding on the large per-patient cost gap between early (EM) and disseminated/late-stage Lyme disease may be worth checking against your own clinic's time-to-diagnosis patterns, to see whether earlier recognition pathways could be strengthened.

Since Belgium's ICD-10-CM coding has no distinct code for EM or PTLDS and all hospital costs were allocated to the disseminated/late category, this may be worth raising with coding/documentation staff as a possible source of misclassified cost data in similar registries.

Given that informal caregiving hours were reported (notably for disseminated/late LB) but not costed, consider whether your own care-coordination process tracks caregiver involvement for complex Lyme presentations.
policy: Use the per-patient cost multiplier (disseminated/late LB costing roughly 27 times as much per patient as EM in this cohort) together with the study's 2015-2017 incidence basis to construct an explicitly labeled projection of potential savings from earlier-diagnosis interventions, since the document itself does not compute this projection.

Consider the reimbursed-versus-patient-paid cost split (about three-quarters reimbursed, about one-quarter patient-paid in this cohort) when evaluating cost-sharing policy for Lyme disease coverage in Belgium.

When citing the roughly €5.59 million national annual estimate, note it blends a 2015-2017 ambulatory incidence basis with a 2016-2018 hospital-admission basis and that the authors flag 2019 as an atypically low tick-bite year, so treat it as an approximate rather than a precise single-year figure for budgeting.

package.documentation:
## Source
This simulator is based on Geebelen et al. (BMC Public Health, 2022), a Belgian prospective-cohort (HUMTICK) and hospital-registry cost-of-illness study of Lyme borreliosis (LB), covering erythema migrans (EM, early rash) and disseminated/late LB (including post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, PTLDS). All monetary figures are 2019 euros from a societal perspective, capturing direct medical, direct non-medical (travel, paid help), and productivity-loss costs up to 6 months post-diagnosis (12 months for PTLDS).

## Parameters
Case counts (EM: 11,168/year; disseminated/late LB: 673/year) reflect average 2015-2017 annual LB incidence applied to the 2019 Belgian population, as used in the document's own national cost table. Per-patient mean costs (EM: €193; disseminated/late LB: €5,148) and the reimbursed-cost share (75.5%) are observed values from the document's Results and Discussion sections. The national total output multiplies each subgroup's own case count by that subgroup's own per-patient cost and sums the two, mirroring the document's table structure; this recomputation lands close to but not exactly at the document's own stated €5.59 million total, and that small discrepancy is not explained by the document itself.

## Limitations
Hospital costs were identified using ICD-10-CM codes in Belgium's mandatory hospital registry; because no distinct code exists for EM or PTLDS, all hospital costs were allocated to the disseminated/late LB category, and coding quality could not be verified - so figures involving hospitalization likely undercount or misattribute true EM/PTLDS-specific costs. All headline figures are pooled national values with no breakdown by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; the document does not report checking for such variation, though federal survey instruments such as NHIS or BRFSS generally support disaggregated analysis even though this study did not perform one. Separately, Belgium's hospital coding system itself lacks a pathway to distinguish EM/PTLDS presentations from other disseminated/late LB hospitalizations, a system-level gap distinct from the accuracy of the cost estimate itself. Other noted gaps: no costs beyond the 6-12 month follow-up window, pediatric costs assumed equal to adult costs (unverified), small PTLDS samples (6 EM-PTLDS, 3 disseminated-PTLDS patients), unvalued informal caregiving time, and excluded non-reimbursed hospital supplements and tick-bite prophylaxis costs. Mean-based totals differ from median patient experience due to cost skew reported in the source. Figures are Belgium-specific and should not be transposed to other healthcare systems or currencies without explicit adjustment.

spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces the per-patient and national annual cost figures reported by a Belgian prospective cohort and hospital-registry cost-of-illness study of erythema migrans (EM, early Lyme rash) versus disseminated/late Lyme borreliosis (including post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, PTLDS). takeaway.patient: Using this Belgian study's own reported figures, a patient diagnosed with disseminated or late-stage Lyme disease had a typical total cost (medical care, travel, and lost income combined) several times higher than a patient diagnosed with the early rash stage (erythema migrans), and about a quarter of direct medical costs were not reimbursed by insurance in this cohort.
takeaway.care: This scenario shows that per-patient costs for disseminated/late-stage Lyme borreliosis far exceed those for early-stage erythema migrans in this Belgian cohort, and that Belgium's hospital coding system cannot separately capture EM or PTLDS hospital presentations - both findings are relevant to how early-detection pathways and diagnosis coding are structured.
takeaway.policy: This scenario reproduces the study's national annual cost estimate for Lyme borreliosis in Belgium by combining each disease-stage subgroup's own case count and per-patient cost, showing that disseminated/late-stage disease drives the majority of national cost despite being far less common than early-stage disease, and quantifies the reimbursed-versus-patient-paid cost split relevant to coverage policy.

patient: Review your own medical bills and insurance statements to see how much of your Lyme-related medical costs were reimbursed versus paid out of pocket, since this study found roughly a quarter of direct medical costs were not reimbursed in this Belgian cohort.

If you have questions about why your stage of diagnosis (early rash versus later/disseminated disease) affects your costs or care plan, consider raising this directly with your clinician in plain terms rather than assuming a specific cause.

If you or a family member provided unpaid caregiving time during treatment, know that this study documented such caregiving but did not assign it a dollar value, so your own experience of that burden may not be reflected in these cost figures.
care: This finding on the large per-patient cost gap between early (EM) and disseminated/late-stage Lyme disease may be worth checking against your own clinic's time-to-diagnosis patterns, to see whether earlier recognition pathways could be strengthened.

Since Belgium's ICD-10-CM coding has no distinct code for EM or PTLDS and all hospital costs were allocated to the disseminated/late category, this may be worth raising with coding/documentation staff as a possible source of misclassified cost data in similar registries.
